newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania plans rules to boost local debt markets.
newsitem.headline: Romania plans rules to boost local debt markets.

text.p: Romania plans to issue this month new rules to boost security trading on its primary and secondary markets, as well as improve domestic public debt management, a finance ministry official said on Friday.
"We will soon start to place our domestic issues through auctions, besides the current public subscription sessions," public debt department manager Mihai Tanasescu told Reuters.
"There will also be new rules for their trading on the secondary market and we are seeking to consolidate public debt by launching longer maturity papers," he added.
Romania has so far financed the bulk of its budget deficits by issuing leu- or dollar-denominated treasury bills.

But most paper had 90-day maturity, pressing the ministry to launch several rollover bills. With an almost absent secondary market, the ministry had tried to offer attractive returns to secure bills' placement through the central bank.

Turning to the auction system would lend more flexibility to the primary market, where banks and financial institutions would act as primary dealers, Tanasescu said. "Primary dealers will be keen to develop a secondary market to boost liquidity".
The market will be opened to commercial banks operating in Romania as well as to corporate residents.
The total outstanding domestic bills on the Romanian market amount to 4.2 trillion lei. Internal public debt was 6.69 trillion lei at end-1996.

Total volume on the secondary market was a mere 213 bills on turnover of 2.13 billion lei in March, but operators expect active trading this month with declining money market rates making investments in fixed-coupon T-bills more attractive.
Latest BNR data put secondary market volume at a record 877 papers this week on overall turnover of 8.8 billion lei.
Offered yields, calculated at the average auctioned rate, stayed high in recent months, at up to 290 percent, prompting analysts to call that a "costly" choice burdening the budget.
Recent tough monetary policies pushed the auctioned rate to an all-time peak of 426 percent in February before it bounced back to 190 percent this week.

Traders said that despite a recent slip in yields towards 196 percent, they remained better than placements on the money market, which trades mostly shorter-maturity funds. One-week money market prices were near 180 percent.

A decision on the type of bills to be issued shortly is expected by mid-April. Romania first issued T-bills in 1994, starting with discount-bills, followed by fixed- or floating-coupon T-bills. ($=6,991 lei)
